newsitem.title: USA: CBOT panel cites surge in soy prices on stocks.
newsitem.headline: CBOT panel cites surge in soy prices on stocks.

text.p: Soybean futures were expected to surge 10 to 20 cents per bushel higher on the Chicago Board of Trade open Friday following the release of a government Supply/Demand Report and amid analysts' forcasts for future cuts in estimates of South American soybean production.

"Reports coming in indicate those crops (South American soy) will be lowered and I think they're lower than what USDA is showing," said Bob Lekberg, grain and oilseed analyst for Chicago-based trade house Goldenberg Hehmeyer and Co.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture in its April supply/demand data early Friday, left unchanged from its March report its estimate for Brazil's soybean production this year at 27.0 million tonnes. Also, USDA only slightly trimmed its outlook for Argentina's production to 13.25 million tonnes from the previous government estimate for 13.5 million tonnes.

"Most (analysts) are indicating a cut in the Argentine crop, a lot are estimating it at 12.0 million to 12.5 million tonnes and that's about where we are," said Daniel Basse, executive vice president of AgResource, Inc.

Basse, speaking on a CBOT-sponsored panel after the report, said he expects CBOT soybean futures to open 15 to 20 cents per bushel higher, corn two to four cents higher and wheat, three to six cents higher.
Soybeans were seen boosted by USDA's cut Friday to 125 million bushels from the previous 140 million its estimate for 1996-97 U.S. soybean ending stocks. The 1996-97 marketing year ends on August 31.
Analysts had expected USDA to leave the ending stocks tally unchanged or trim only five to 10 million bushels from its previous outlook.

USDA cut its U.S. corn ending stocks estimate to 909 million bushels from its previous outlook of 959 million. The agency also trimmed the U.S. wheat ending stocks number to 460 million bushels from the previous 474 million.
The panelists said the downward adjustments in grain and soybean ending stocks suggest 1996 U.S. crop production may not have been as large as previously reported.
"It strongly suggests USDA overestimated last year's crop," Basse said.
"The wheat number was pretty close to expected" but the market will be looking out for cold in the Plains this weekend and cold and wet corn planting conditions," Basse said.

"We do have the dynamics changing quite a bit for wheat," Lekberg said. "There's a potential disruption in plantings in the northern U.S. spring wheat area and cold weather is coming into the winter (hard red winter) area."
